teaser: Delacroix spent a few hours in a room no stranger was meant to see. Painters never forgot it.
review_notes:
Visit to Algiers in June 1832 (about three days) on the return from the Mornay mission to Morocco; access arranged by the harbor engineer Victor Poirel through a former corsair captain: traditional account, details debated.
Names Mouney and Zohra Bensoltane from inscriptions on the watercolor sketches.
Salon of 1834, bought by King Louis-Philippe.
Dimensions about 180 x 229 cm.
Second version of 1849 at the Musee Fabre, Montpellier.
Picasso's 15 variations (1954-55); “Version O” sold for about $179 million in 2015.
Cezanne's remark about the slippers is paraphrased, not quoted.
Photo shows some glare and a dark upper centre; details there were not used.

lesson.text: How do you paint a place you were never supposed to enter? In 1832 the women's quarters of a Muslim home in Algiers were closed to any man outside the family, and above all to a visiting Frenchman. Delacroix got in anyway, for a few hours. This painting is what he carried out.

He was on his way home from Morocco, where he had traveled for six months with a French diplomatic mission. The ship stopped in Algiers for about three days. France had invaded the city just two years earlier. A harbor engineer is said to have persuaded a local sea captain to let the painter visit his household.

Delacroix sketched fast in watercolor, noting colors in the margins and even the women's names: Mouney and Zohra. Back in Paris he worked for two years, with French models wearing clothes he had brought back, to turn those pages into a canvas nearly 2.3 meters wide (about 7.5 feet).
The trip produced seven notebooks crammed with drawings and notes. Delacroix drew on them for the rest of his life: he was still painting North African subjects thirty years later.

The result is strangely quiet. Nothing happens. Three women sit on rugs in a dim, tiled room while a servant leaves. If there is a story, it is told by small things lying around, and one pair of them shows how relaxed the room is.
Someone has kicked off her shoes. Where did they land?

spots.title: The slippers
spots.text: Red and gold slippers lie abandoned on the tiles at the bottom edge, pointing different ways. The painter Cézanne later said their red went into the eye like a glass of wine down the throat.

lesson.text: Bare feet, shoes left where they fell: these women are at home, not posing. That was new. Earlier European pictures of the “harem” were fantasies of dancers and bathers, invented by men who had seen nothing. Delacroix's room has boredom in it, and heat, and time passing slowly.
He still looks as an outsider, and a guest of the occupying power. The painting is both a rare firsthand record and a European's dream of the East, and it is honest to keep both in mind.

What struck Parisians at the Salon of 1834 was the color. Delacroix had come back from North Africa convinced that shadows are not gray or brown but full of colored reflections, and that colors grow stronger when their opposites sit beside them.

Check this for yourself in the painting. Reds are set against greens, oranges against blues, in small touches. And the light falls from the upper left, so the woman nearest the source glows while the far corner sinks into warm darkness.

King Louis-Philippe bought the painting straight from the Salon for the national collection. Fifteen years later Delacroix painted the room again, smaller and dimmer, as if seen through memory. That second version is in Montpellier.

Later painters treated this canvas as a textbook. Renoir painted his own Algerian women in tribute. Signac, a leader of the painters who built pictures from dots of pure color, studied its little paired touches as proof that Delacroix had got there first.
Between 1954 and 1955 Picasso painted fifteen variations on it, lettered A to O. In 2015 the last one, “Version O,” sold at auction for about 179 million dollars, a world record at the time.
The room is yours now, without a guide. Wander through it at your own pace, the way Delacroix could not: he had only hours, and you have as long as you like.

spots.title: The woman at left
spots.text: She leans on a cushion in full light and is the only one who looks toward us. Pearls circle her neck, and her jacket is edged in gold on orange.

spots.title: The middle figure
spots.text: Seated cross-legged, she turns to her companion as if mid-sentence. A yellow scarf at her throat sits against the blue cloth on her lap.

spots.title: The rose
spots.text: A pink rose is pinned in black hair, above a face lowered in shadow. The cheek is modeled with soft pinks and cool tones, not with brown.

spots.title: The water pipe
spots.text: A hookah, a pipe that cools smoke through water, stands on the floor with its tube looping up to the third woman's hand. Beside it sits a small brazier of coals.

spots.title: The servant
spots.text: She walks out to the right, glancing back over her shoulder, one hand lifting the heavy curtain. Her striped skirt and blue vest are among the strongest colors in the picture.

spots.title: The red doors
spots.text: A wall cupboard with red lattice doors stands half open, with glassware on the shelf above. Its red answers the greens and blues of the tiles around it.

spots.title: The mirror
spots.text: A mirror in a curling gilt frame tilts from the wall and reflects only a sliver of light. It shows nothing of the room, and nothing of the painter.

spots.title: Signed and dated
spots.text: In the bottom right corner, on the checkered floor: “Eug. Delacroix” and the year 1834, when the picture was shown in Paris.

quiz.question: Why was Delacroix's visit so unusual?
options: The women's quarters were closed to outside men
He was only twelve years old
quiz.explanation: A stranger, and a foreigner, was normally never admitted to that part of a home.

quiz.question: How long was his stop in Algiers?
quiz.explanation: He stopped there briefly on the way back from Morocco.

quiz.question: What did North Africa teach him about shadows?
options: That they should be painted pure black
That they do not exist in strong sun
That they are full of colored reflections
quiz.explanation: He came back convinced shadows hold color, not just gray or brown.

quiz.question: What lies abandoned at the bottom edge of the picture?
quiz.explanation: Red and gold slippers were kicked off onto the tiles.

quiz.question: Which artist painted fifteen variations on this work in the 1950s?
quiz.explanation: Picasso's series runs from Version A to Version O.

facts.text: Delacroix painted the final canvas on the spot, inside the house in Algiers.
facts.explanation: He made quick watercolor sketches there and painted the canvas in Paris over two years.

facts.text: The French king bought the painting from the Salon of 1834.
facts.explanation: Louis-Philippe purchased it for the national collection.

facts.text: The mirror on the wall shows Delacroix's reflection.
facts.explanation: It reflects only a sliver of light and shows nothing of the painter.
